origin_region: Yunnan (pu-erh), Fujian (aged white tea and Wuyi oolong), Guangdong (aged Dancong), Hunan and Guangxi (dark teas); Taiwan (aged oolong); stored in Kunming, Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Taiwan and Malaysia
processing: Ageing is storage, not a factory step: over years, slow oxidation, residual enzyme activity and, in post-fermented teas, microbial activity change the leaf's chemistry. Teas that age well are those finished without a high-temperature 'kill' of their enzymes or with a microbial component: sheng pu-erh, heicha, white tea (especially pressed), heavily roasted oolongs (re-roasted every few years) and some black teas. Green teas and light oolongs do not age; they go stale.
harvest_season: Any; what matters is the year of production and the years in storage, and both should be stated.
appearance_dry: Leaf darkens with age: a sheng cake goes from green-grey to brown and red-brown over a decade or two, white tea from silver-green to brown, roasted oolong from dark brown to near black.
appearance_liquor: Deepens from pale yellow to orange, amber and finally red-brown, staying clear in well-stored tea; a murky cup suggests damp storage.
appearance_wet: Supple brown to dark-brown leaf; wet-stored tea is darker, softer and smells of cellar.
taste_profile: Bitterness and astringency fade while honey, dried fruit, wood, camphor and medicinal or incense notes build; well-aged tea is smooth, sweet, deep and long rather than loud, and the storage climate (dry Kunming, humid Hong Kong or Malaysia) shapes the result as much as the years.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, a quick rinse (two for wet-stored tea), short steeps and many of them; aged tea rewards a thick clay pot and keeps giving long after a young tea has faded. Let a freshly unwrapped cake breathe for a few weeks after it arrives from storage.

vintage_note: This is the one category where the year is everything, and also where it is most often faked. Sheng pu-erh is sold by production year, as young (1–3 years), mid-aged (roughly 5–15) and aged (15–30+), with the factory, recipe number, wrapper and storage history all part of the price; most honest 'aged' tea on the market is from 1995 onward and anything claiming the 1950s–80s needs provenance. White tea is sold as 1-, 3-, 7- and 10-year-plus cakes under the saying 'one year tea, three years medicine, seven years treasure', which is marketing, not pharmacology. Aged oolongs are sold with the harvest year and the dates of re-roasting; aged heicha by batch year. Dry-stored, natural-stored and traditional (humid) storage should be declared.
description:
Ageing is what happens to certain teas when you leave them alone: over years in a cupboard, a warehouse or a Hong Kong basement, the bitter, green, aggressive compounds of a young leaf slowly transform into sweetness, depth and the woody, camphor-like, medicinal aromas that collectors pay for. It applies only to teas whose chemistry is still alive, raw and ripe pu-erh, other dark teas, white tea, heavily roasted oolongs and a few blacks; a green tea left for ten years is not aged, it is dead.

The changes are slow oxidation, leftover enzyme activity and, in post-fermented teas, the work of microbes that live in the leaf, and they depend heavily on climate. The same cake stored dry in Kunming stays bright and slow; stored in humid Guangzhou or Hong Kong it darkens and softens fast and picks up a cellar note; stored in Malaysia it lands somewhere in between. There is no single correct storage, only a declared one, and 'wet storage' pushed too far produces mould rather than age.

A well-aged tea tastes smooth, sweet and deep, with dried fruit, wood, honey and camphor and a cooling feeling in the throat, and it keeps going for a dozen steeps or more. Brew it with boiling water, rinse it, and use short steeps in a clay pot; the usual mistake is to be timid with temperature. A cake fresh out of storage often needs a few weeks of air to shake off a flat, closed note.

Buying aged tea is buying a story, so the story needs evidence: the year, the factory or maker, the recipe or batch, the wrapper and the storage history. Fake 'antique' cakes with convincing old wrappers are the biggest fraud in tea; genuine aged tea from the 1990s and 2000s is widely available and is the sensible place to start. Aged white tea cakes, sold by year since the mid-2000s, are the cheaper way to taste what a decade does to a leaf.

Try a young and a ten-year-old sheng from the same region side by side, and then a dry-stored and a humid-stored cake of similar age: those two comparisons teach more than any description.
